title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.method_basis: The 6956 key of Biermann and Bosbach (DECODE R215), extended in this batch with about 125 nomenclator groups learnt from the Roman decipherments Kiewning printed in 1897, decodes the sheets; where Kiewning prints a sheet verbatim the reading follows the print, elsewhere it is read from the figures checked on the DECODE scans.
outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.method_basis: The 6956 key of Biermann and Bosbach (DECODE R215), extended in this batch with about 125 nomenclator groups learnt from the Roman decipherments Kiewning printed in 1897, decodes the sheets; where Kiewning prints a sheet verbatim the reading follows the print, elsewhere it is read from the figures checked on the DECODE scans.
outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.method_basis: The 6956 key of Biermann and Bosbach (DECODE R215), extended in this batch with about 125 nomenclator groups learnt from the Roman decipherments Kiewning printed in 1897, decodes the sheets; where Kiewning prints a sheet verbatim the reading follows the print, elsewhere it is read from the figures checked on the DECODE scans.
outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.method_basis: The 6956 key of Biermann and Bosbach (DECODE R215), extended in this batch with about 125 nomenclator groups learnt from the Roman decipherments Kiewning printed in 1897, decodes the sheets; where Kiewning prints a sheet verbatim the reading follows the print, elsewhere it is read from the figures checked on the DECODE scans.
outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.method_basis: The 6956 key of Biermann and Bosbach (DECODE R215), extended in this batch with about 125 nomenclator groups learnt from the Roman decipherments Kiewning printed in 1897, decodes the sheets; where Kiewning prints a sheet verbatim the reading follows the print, elsewhere it is read from the figures checked on the DECODE scans.
outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 - 28 ciphered despatches of the nuncio at Vienna (BAV, Barb.lat. 6960)
system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.
system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.verification: contemporary decipherment; key confirms; historical consistency
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

title: Janos Papai (Constantinople) to Ferenc Rakoczi II, 1706-1710, in the envoy key R580 (DECODE R740, R741, R757, R765, R784, R793-R796, R805, R823)
system.summary: Hungarian syllabic nomenclator, values 10-322: two homophones per letter, CV/VC syllables, and names, countries, places and months.
system.sibling_key: DECODE R580 / R581 / R452 (Papai Janosnak adott Clavis)
system.notes: Key heading: Nemzetes Vitezlo Papai Janosnak adott Clavis massa. R731 (1710) uses a separate graphic-sign alphabet and has its own entry (papai1710).
conditions.prior_solution.where: DECODE marked R805 partly decrypted (interlinear syllables); Benda's 1963 edition of Papai's Turkish diaries not checked
conditions.human_role: Posed the target; supplied the DECODE session cookie earlier.
conditions.tools: DECODE record metadata search; table decoder
outcome.method_basis: DECODE key R580/R581, headed 'key given to János Pápai', from the same Rákóczi archive (MNL OL G15), was applied to DECODE's transcriptions of the eleven numeric letters and read 99.7% of groups.
outcome.contribution: transcription; key extended or corrected; sender or date identified; catalogue correction
outcome.notes: Eleven numeric letters read at 99.7% of groups after the second pass; 57 scattered groups (DECODE digit slips) and ~41 '?' tokens open, all blocked by the transcription. Split 14 Oct 2026: R731's graphic-sign passages are papai1710; on the eleven letters alone the read bar is met, so the class is read (was read in part).

title: William Perwich to Lord Arlington, Paris, 9 April 1670, TNA SP 78/129 f. 180
system.summary: Columnar transposition with 20 columns, each written out as a line padded with nulls, framed by two null lines, with a few numeric nomenclator codes inside the plaintext.
system.sibling_key: none used
system.notes: Key as transcribed row numbers in plaintext column order: 15 20 19 17 18 21 16 14 2 4 3 5 6 7 13 12 11 10 9 8. Nulls: 47 column-tail cells plus the two null lines (23 + 9 cells). Nomenclator entries counted from the plaintext (40, 60, 61, 96, 97); 910 and 192 sit in the null tails.
conditions.prior_solution.where: TNA blog, 14 Oct 2025: broken independently by Matthew Brown and by Lasry, Biermann and Tomokiyo; plaintext in plaintext_tna.txt
conditions.human_role: Project-level: obtained a DECODE login with privileges and passed its session cookie (from the browser developer tools) to the model, set up Claude Code with Fable 5.1 or Opus 5, and posed the problem with /goal; occasionally offered encouragement or chose which of the model-identified leads to pursue. No target-specific intervention recorded.
conditions.tools: quadgram hill-climber over column order (solve20.py); chi-squared and digram-repeat tests (grid.py, routes.py); substitution solvers (masc.py, stream.py, segclimb.py)
outcome.method_basis: A complete decipherment already existed: the TNA published the plaintext on 14 Oct 2025 (Matthew Brown; Lasry, Biermann and Tomokiyo). The column order was reproduced here from Tomokiyo's transcription only after that announcement had given the system, and the project's own earlier substitution attack had failed.
outcome.notes: Solved by others in Oct 2025; this project first argued, wrongly, that it was a substitution, then reproduced the published break. The transposition key is complete; the nomenclator numbers are unread (40 probably a place, 60 96 and 61 persons). TNA context readings of the codes: 97 the Dutch, 60 and 61 the King, 96 Colbert, 40 England. No write-up: deciphered by others first (a page made 24 Sept 2026 was withdrawn the same day).

outcome.notes: All digit pairs map. Writer Prince Frederick, late Nov - early Dec 1795.

title: Ranzo's code, 1528: the letter to 'Garbino' (BnF fr. 3022 no. 20, Madrid 11 April 1528) and Hieronimo Ranzo's letters (fr. 2988 ff. 2, 9-10; DECODE R1894, R4450)
system.summary: Initial-letter code: each group is the initial of a word or syllable with a number (c170 che, i100 il, p149 per); numbering within a letter not alphabetical; z-groups nulls or punctuation. The 'Aditione nel zifra' bound with no. 20 (fr. 3022 f. 50) is of the same design but belongs to another code: only 1 of its 113 groups occurs in these letters.
system.sibling_key: No. 20 shares its code with Ranzo's signed letters in fr. 2988 and fr. 3019 no. 27; no contemporary key found. Keys rebuilt by Rosson (6 Oct 2026) and George Lasry (6 Oct 2026).
system.notes: numbering tested not alphabetical (n20/alphatest.py, z = -0.5 vs +6.5 on an alphabetical control), hence key_order random for no. 20. z-groups behave as nulls or punctuation. Split 14 Oct 2026 from targets/vasto1527 (del Vasto's letters are in different ciphers).
conditions.prior_solution.where: Rosson (with Claude) 6 Oct 2026, centurione-1528 page: a key for Ranzo's code (no. 20 and fr. 2988 ff. 9-10), built on this project's transcription, found 14 Oct 2026 by a Cryptoole alert, after this project had closed no. 20 as unread. George Lasry reports independent contemporaneous recovery with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, based on Norbert Biermann's transcription (contributed 14 Oct 2026). Cryptiana ranzo.htm (6 Oct 2026) records both. Lasry, 16 Oct 2026, by email to Daniel Bourdeau: 'the Ranzo ciphers are solved Fr 2988 and Fr 20506 - my key or Rosson's key'.
conditions.human_role: Project-level: obtained a DECODE login with privileges and passed its session cookie (from the browser developer tools) to the model, set up Claude Code with Fable 5.1 or Opus 5, and posed the problem with /goal; occasionally offered encouragement or chose which of the model-identified leads to pursue. No target-specific intervention recorded.
conditions.tools: word-substitution annealer with Kneser-Ney word-bigram Italian LM (n20/solve2.py); alphabetical-order test with power check (n20/alphatest.py); annealers assuming alphabetical order (n20/solve.py, anchor.py, free.py); calibration on encoded Castiglione control (n20/calib.py)
outcome.method_basis: George Lasry rebuilt his key from the ciphertext of Biermann's five-letter transcription with Italian cribs, repeated contexts and code-family structure (lasry/NOTES.md; PR #35); no decipherment, clear copy or key of these letters exists, and the 'Aditione nel zifra' he spot-checked is another code (1 of its 113 groups occurs here), so no external or adjacent plaintext supplied values. Paolo Rosson rebuilt a second key the same way, independently, on this project's transcription (6 Oct 2026); it agrees with Lasry's on 94-96% of the tokens both value, including letters 4 and 5, which Rosson never saw. This project's own annealer recovered only function words; its share is the transcription and the measurement.
outcome.verification: historical consistency; independent verification; statistical test
outcome.notes: Key recovered from ciphertext-only by George Lasry (with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra) and, independently, by Paolo Rosson (with Claude), both 6 Oct 2026. Lasry, 16 Oct 2026: 'the Ranzo ciphers are solved Fr 2988 and Fr 20506 - my key or Rosson's key'. Measured here 18 Oct 2026: fr. 2988 (both letters) and its copy fr. 20506 meet the read bar; fr. 3022 no. 20, fr. 4050 and fr. 6638 are read in part. Split 14 Oct 2026 from targets/vasto1527. 22 Oct 2026, reading audit: letter 4 (fr. 4050) decoded, not read; fraction_read 0.929 -> 0.717. 23 Oct 2026, re-reading: letter 4 joined into words by hand with Lasry's key, Rosson's key and the code list's rough alphabetical order (39 sense-only values flagged); it reads (B); fraction_read 0.717 -> 0.929.

doc.date: March 1528 (date of the original, fr. 2988 ff. 9-10)
doc.plaintext.source: Read through its original: George Lasry names fr. 20506 ff. 136-138 as the parallel copy of his letter 2 (lasry/transcription.json, counts.json, source.json) and on 16 Oct 2026 wrote that 'the Ranzo ciphers are solved Fr 2988 and Fr 20506 - my key or Rosson's key'. Letter 2's counts apply: 1,728 of 1,781 (97.0%) read by the bar measure (see r1894). Measured 18 Oct 2026 with measure_lasry.py on Lasry's lasry/alignment.tsv (Biermann's transcription), Lasry's key first and Rosson's second: a token is read when it is a presumed null, one of Lasry's stronger inferences, a tentative value of Lasry's that Rosson's independent key matches, or a sure/probable value of Rosson's where Lasry has none.
doc.transcription.source: Norbert Biermann, Ranzo transcript.docx (2021), supplied by George Lasry: letter 2, whose line layout is that of fr. 2988 ff. 9-10; fr. 20506 is listed as its parallel copy
doc.transcription.notes: No separate transcription of fr. 20506 exists here or in Lasry's package; token count is letter 2's (lasry/counts.json: 1,781 occurrences, 35 presumed nulls, 1,703 valued, 43 unassigned). The copy's own variants are not checked against the Gallica images. DECODE R4450 was described here as a copy of f. 9 only; Lasry's source list gives ff. 136-138 for the whole letter.

system.summary: Initial-letter code: each group is the initial of a word or syllable with a number (c170 che, i100 il, p149 per); numbering within a letter not alphabetical; z-groups nulls or punctuation. The 'Aditione nel zifra' bound with no. 20 (fr. 3022 f. 50) is of the same design but belongs to another code: only 1 of its 113 groups occurs in these letters.
system.sibling_key: No. 20 shares its code with Ranzo's signed letters in fr. 2988 and fr. 3019 no. 27; no contemporary key found. Keys rebuilt by Rosson (6 Oct 2026) and George Lasry (6 Oct 2026).
system.notes: numbering tested not alphabetical (n20/alphatest.py, z = -0.5 vs +6.5 on an alphabetical control), hence key_order random for no. 20. z-groups behave as nulls or punctuation. Split 14 Oct 2026 from targets/vasto1527 (del Vasto's letters are in different ciphers).

outcome.method_basis: George Lasry rebuilt his key from the ciphertext of Biermann's five-letter transcription with Italian cribs, repeated contexts and code-family structure (lasry/NOTES.md; PR #35); no decipherment, clear copy or key of these letters exists, and the 'Aditione nel zifra' he spot-checked is another code (1 of its 113 groups occurs here), so no external or adjacent plaintext supplied values. Paolo Rosson rebuilt a second key the same way, independently, on this project's transcription (6 Oct 2026); it agrees with Lasry's on 94-96% of the tokens both value, including letters 4 and 5, which Rosson never saw. This project's own annealer recovered only function words; its share is the transcription and the measurement.

system.summary: Initial-letter code: each group is the initial of a word or syllable with a number (c170 che, i100 il, p149 per); numbering within a letter not alphabetical; z-groups nulls or punctuation. system.sibling_key: No. 20 shares its code with Ranzo's signed letters in fr. 2988 and fr. 3019 no. 27; no contemporary key found. Keys rebuilt by Rosson (6 Oct 2026) and George Lasry (6 Oct 2026).
system.notes: numbering tested not alphabetical (n20/alphatest.py, z = -0.5 vs +6.5 on an alphabetical control), hence key_order random for no. 20. z-groups behave as nulls or punctuation. Split 14 Oct 2026 from targets/vasto1527 (del Vasto's letters are in different ciphers).
conditions.prior_solution.where: Rosson (with Claude) 6 Oct 2026, centurione-1528 page: a key for Ranzo's code (no. 20 and fr. 2988 ff. 9-10), built on this project's transcription, found 14 Oct 2026 by a Cryptoole alert, after this project had closed no. 20 as unread. outcome.method_basis: George Lasry rebuilt his key from the ciphertext of Biermann's five-letter transcription with Italian cribs, repeated contexts and code-family structure (lasry/NOTES.md; PR #35); no decipherment, clear copy or key of these letters exists, and the 'Aditione nel zifra' he spot-checked is another code (1 of its 113 groups occurs here), so no external or adjacent plaintext supplied values. Paolo Rosson rebuilt a second key the same way, independently, on this project's transcription (6 Oct 2026); it agrees with Lasry's on 94-96% of the tokens both value, including letters 4 and 5, which Rosson never saw. This project's own annealer recovered only function words; its share is the transcription and the measurement.

title: Nevers to Revol, Aug-Oct 1593, BnF fr. 3985 and fr. 3986, in the Court symbol cipher no. 60 (catalogue item 21, part)
system.summary: Court symbol cipher no. 60 (Montereau, Aug 1593): a symbol alphabet with about five homophones per letter, a syllabary, Roman-numeral names and places, word signs and nulls.
system.sibling_key: Key no. 60 checked on the interlined Henri IV letter of 7 Oct 1593 (fr. 3986 f. 151) and the interlined Instruction of 31 Aug (fr. 3985 c. 264-268).
system.notes: Split 14 Oct 2026 from nevers1593. The copyist's cursive forms differ from the Court hand of the table; atlas60.md collects them.
conditions.prior_solution.where: Tomokiyo (cryptiana henryiv2.htm) decoded three words of f. 146v (l'absolution, a la verite, interest) and guessed 'conversion' on f. 88r

conditions.human_role: Project-level: obtained a DECODE login with privileges and passed its session cookie (from the browser developer tools) to the model, set up Claude Code with Fable 5.1 or Opus 5, and posed the problem with /goal; occasionally offered encouragement or chose which of the model-identified leads to pursue. No target-specific intervention recorded.
conditions.tools: decode60.py; f88/shuffle_control.py
outcome.method_basis: Key no. 60, the Court cipher given to Nevers (BnF fr. 3995 ff. 108-111), identified by Tomokiyo and applied (read with known key, recorded under parts), gives three words on f. 88r and anchors on f. 146v; no passage reads as text. Method restored 24 Oct 2026 (George Lasry: a key can be mostly recovered while the text is not read): the key was obtained by key no. 60, the Court cipher given to Nevers, identified by Tomokiyo; class stays not read, as the text does not read.
outcome.notes: Read in part only on f. 88r; the blocker so far is palaeographic (the copyist's cursive forms), and three passages are still to transcribe (Status: in progress). 23 Oct 2026, re-read (b15): no contemporary or printed text of ff. 88, 146v, 157v; f. 146v re-read at full resolution without a reading; all three stay decoded, not read (texts/f88-f146v-f157v_reread_log.md).

title: Charles Hémard de Denonville, cardinal de Mâcon, Rome and Orvieto to Anne de Montmorency, 1536-37, in Mascon's cipher (BnF fr. 3053, DECODE R4233-R4247; BnF fr. 3071 no. 4)
system.summary: Homophonic substitution on digit-like graphic signs, one sign per letter, with doubled-letter signs, nulls and three two-digit code groups.
system.sibling_key: 'Mascon's cipher' as reconstructed by S. Tomokiyo from fr. 3053 and tabulated by G. Lasry (2023) for BnF fr. 3071 f. 9; working table macon_key.md (moved here from targets/gramont1529/), used with corrections.
system.notes: Code groups 20 = l'Empereur, 30 = pape, 40 = roy, and no others in the seven fr. 3053 records or the fr. 3071 letter. The barred-cross family of signs reads F, P, O, U, V and D in the same hand and is separable only by context; the big curly X is Q/U, not N, contrary to the working table. distinct_symbols counts the fr. 3053 records. The f. 85 record (R4248) is in a second, unrelated fr. 3053 cipher and is its own entry since 14 Oct 2026 (targets/r4248/).

title: Charles Hémard de Denonville, cardinal de Mâcon, Rome and Orvieto to Anne de Montmorency, 1536-37, in Mascon's cipher (BnF fr. 3053, DECODE R4233-R4247; BnF fr. 3071 no. 4)
system.summary: Homophonic substitution on digit-like graphic signs, one sign per letter, with doubled-letter signs, nulls and three two-digit code groups.
system.sibling_key: 'Mascon's cipher' as reconstructed by S. Tomokiyo from fr. 3053 and tabulated by G. Lasry (2023) for BnF fr. 3071 f. 9; working table macon_key.md (moved here from targets/gramont1529/), used with corrections.
system.notes: Code groups 20 = l'Empereur, 30 = pape, 40 = roy, and no others in the seven fr. 3053 records or the fr. 3071 letter. The barred-cross family of signs reads F, P, O, U, V and D in the same hand and is separable only by context; the big curly X is Q/U, not N, contrary to the working table. distinct_symbols counts the fr. 3053 records. The f. 85 record (R4248) is in a second, unrelated fr. 3053 cipher and is its own entry since 14 Oct 2026 (targets/r4248/).
conditions.prior_solution.where: Contemporary marginal and interlinear decipherments of some fr. 3053 passages in the volume itself, and the slip f. 9bis deciphering the f. 9v passage of fr. 3071 no. 4. No printed or online plaintext: Tomokiyo and Lasry publish the key only. Lasry also decoded fr. 3071 no. 4 in 2023, unpublished (Lasry, 21 Sept 2026); no Lasry decipherment of the fr. 3053 letters is recorded.

conditions.human_role: nothing beyond setting the target; the DECODE session cookie already in the repository served the images
